anchor: her feet trotted along beneath her
title: Eurycleia's eager old legs
greek: γούνατα δ' ἐρρώσαντο, πόδες δ' ὑπερικταίνοντο (gounata d' errōsanto, podes d' huperiktainonto)
short: The old nurse hurries upstairs laughing, her knees moving briskly and her feet tripping beneath her: a rare comic touch with a word found nowhere else.
body: Huperiktainonto is unique in Greek. Monro follows Aristarchus in taking it as a compound of hupo, used of the lower limbs, and guesses at a meaning 'bustled' or 'trotted along'; an ancient grammarian connected it instead with ereikō, 'break', explaining it as 'gave way beneath her', which Monro finds unsatisfactory in sense. Errōsanto describes 'a continuous or rhythmical movement' (compare 24.69, of warriors moving round the pyre). Monro aptly compares Virgil's old nurse Barce hurrying with 'an old woman's eagerness' (Aeneid 4.641). The light opening contrasts with Penelope's deep sleep and long disbelief in the scene that follows.

title: Penelope's 'unbelieving heart'
greek: θυμὸς δέ τοι αἰὲν ἄπιστος (thumos de toi aien apistos)
short: Penelope refuses to believe Eurycleia: some god must have killed the suitors, while Odysseus is lost far away. Her caution is the virtue that has kept her faithful.
body: Eurycleia's reproach repeats word for word what the disguised Odysseus said to the doubting Eumaeus (14.150), so the loyal swineherd and the faithful wife share the same hard-won scepticism after twenty years of false reports. Penelope's explanation, that an immortal punished the suitors' outrage (23.63-7), is not foolish: it agrees with what Odysseus himself says about the gods' fate (22.413) and what Medon reports (24.443-9). She later explains her slowness: she always feared that some man would deceive her with words (23.215-17). Her doubt is therefore part of her characterisation as periphrōn, 'very prudent', the mind that matches Odysseus' own. Monro notes the shape of her opening words: a general statement about gods who can make the wise foolish, followed by the particular case, 'even thee' (23.11-14).

title: A heart 'harder than stone', a heart 'of iron'
greek: κραδίη στερεωτέρη ἐστὶ λίθοιο (kradiē stereōterē esti lithoio); σιδήρεον ἦτορ (sidēreon ētor); κῆρ ἀτέραμνον (kēr ateramnon)
short: First Telemachus, then Odysseus himself accuse Penelope of a heart harder than stone and of iron, because she will not embrace the stranger at once.
body: Telemachus' outburst ('cruel mother', mēter dusmēter) and Odysseus' later complaint use the same lines (23.100-2 = 168-70), a repetition that Monro, following Kirchhoff, treats as a sign of awkward composition around the bath scene. The images are traditional: Hecuba tells Priam he has 'a heart of iron' for daring to go to Achilles (Il. 24.205), and Achilles says the same of Priam (Il. 24.521). Here the 'hardness' is misread: Penelope is not unfeeling but cautious, and her reply to her son (23.105-10) explains that she is struck dumb with wonder and will test the stranger by secret signs. The joke is that the man complaining of her hardness of heart is himself the most guarded of heroes.

anchor: signs which we two alone know
title: Secret signs (sēmata) between husband and wife
greek: σήμαθ', ἃ δὴ καὶ νῶϊ κεκρυμμένα ἴδμεν ἀπ' ἄλλων (sēmath', ha dē kai nōi kekrummena idmen ap' allōn)
short: Penelope says that if he is truly Odysseus they will know each other by signs only the two of them know: recognition by shared knowledge, not appearance.
body: Sēma, 'sign, token', is a key word of the last books: the scar is a sēma (21.217, 23.73), the bed contains a 'great sēma' (23.188, 202, 206), and Laertes asks for and receives sēmata (24.329, 346). Unlike the scar, which others can see, Penelope's signs are knowledge hidden from others. Monro notes a metrical anomaly in kekrummena at 23.110, suggesting the line may need emendation, and defends the emphatic kai nōi. Odysseus smiles at her words (23.111), recognising, it seems, a mind like his own. The motif expresses the ideal of homophrosunē, 'like-mindedness' between husband and wife, which Odysseus praised to Nausicaa as the best of blessings (6.180-5).

title: Homicide and exile: the threat of blood-feud
greek: φεύγει πηούς τε προλιπὼν καὶ πατρίδα γαῖαν (pheugei pēous te prolipōn kai patrida gaian); ἕρμα πόληος (herma polēos)
short: Even a man who kills one person with few avengers must flee his country, Odysseus warns; they have killed 'the stay of the city'.
body: In the Homeric world a killer faced vengeance from the victim's kin and usually went into exile, as Patroclus did as a boy (Il. 23.85-90) and the seer Theoclymenus has done (Od. 15.272-8); the great simile of Priam as a fugitive killer arriving at a rich man's house (Il. 24.480-2) draws on the same custom, and Odysseus' false Cretan tale has him fleeing after a killing (13.259-70). Herma polēos, 'the ballast' or 'prop of the city', describes the suitors as the leading families' sons: their deaths will bring their fathers and brothers against Odysseus. This speech sets up the final movement of the poem: the stratagem of the fake wedding, the departure to Laertes' farm, Eupeithes' call for vengeance, and Zeus' imposed amnesty in Book XXIV.

title: The sham wedding dance
greek: ὥς κέν τις φαίη γάμον ἔμμεναι (hōs ken tis phaiē gamon emmenai)
short: To hide the massacre from the town, Odysseus has the bard play for a dance, so that passers-by think Penelope has at last remarried.
body: The ruse buys time before the 'wide report of the killing' (kleos euru phonou) reaches the city (23.137), and it is full of irony. The 'song and lyre' Odysseus promised the suitors as the 'accompaniments of a feast' (21.428-30) are now literally performed over their bodies; the wedding the suitors sought takes place, but between Penelope and her own husband; and the passers-by condemn her as schetliē, 'hard-hearted', 'unfeeling' in Monro's explanation, for not waiting, the opposite of the truth. Monro notes that agros here means 'a farm', as Latin rus. The scene's double meaning shows how the poem uses the institutions of feast, song and marriage that the suitors corrupted to mark the restoration of order.

title: Odysseus' bath and transformation
greek: λοῦσεν καὶ χρῖσεν ἐλαίῳ (lousen kai chrisen elaiōi)
short: Eurynome bathes Odysseus and Athena makes him taller and more beautiful, using the same lines and simile of gold overlaid on silver as in Book VI.
body: Lines 23.157-62 repeat 6.230-5, where Athena beautifies Odysseus for Nausicaa; the craftsman 'whom Hephaestus and Pallas Athena have taught' pours gold round silver. Monro takes this as an enamel or inlay technique of which there are fine Mycenaean examples, and judges the first two repeated lines wrongly inserted. More seriously, he reports Kirchhoff's argument that the bath 'makes an awkward break' in the scene with Penelope and is ignored afterwards: she failed to recognise him in his rags, yet his transformation into splendour passes without comment, whereas a similar change deeply moved Telemachus (16.178-85). Kirchhoff therefore rejected the passage, and Monro thinks he is 'probably right'. Others answer that Penelope's caution is not about appearance at all, so the change is meant not to work.

title: Daimoniē: 'Strange lady!'
greek: δαιμονίη (daimoniē); δαιμόνιε (daimonie)
short: Odysseus addresses Penelope as daimoniē, a form of address expressing exasperated wonder, and she answers him with the same word.
body: Daimonios, from daimōn, 'divinity', is used in address to someone whose behaviour seems inexplicable, as if a god were at work in them; its tone ranges from reproach to affectionate bewilderment, hence Murray's 'Strange lady!' and 'Strange sir'. Hector and Andromache use it to each other in their great farewell (Il. 6.407, 6.486), and Odysseus used it to rebuke the maid Melantho (19.71). Here the exchange is exactly reciprocal: Odysseus says daimoniē at 23.166, Penelope replies daimoni' at 23.174, and he uses it again when she insists on hearing Teiresias' prophecy (23.264). The matching address signals that the two are equals in the contest of wits that leads to the test of the bed.

title: Penelope's test: the movable bed
greek: πόσιος πειρωμένη (posios peirōmenē)
short: Penelope orders Eurycleia to move the bed out of the bridal chamber; Odysseus, stung, reveals that no one could move it without cutting the olive trunk it was built on.
body: The master of disguise and testing is here tested and caught off guard. Monro paraphrases Penelope's carefully ambiguous reply: she is not proud, scornful or offended, nor has she forgotten what he was, 'but if you are Ulysses you will see the meaning of the order', to move the bedstead out of the chamber he himself built. Odysseus responds 'in a burst of anger' (ochthēsas), and it is his emotion, as much as his knowledge, that proves his identity: only the builder would care. The trick reverses the pattern of the poem, in which Odysseus always tests others first; Penelope proves herself his equal in mētis, cunning intelligence, and their reunion becomes a meeting of like minds.

title: The bed built on a living olive tree
greek: θάμνος ἔφυ τανύφυλλος ἐλαίης (thamnos ephu tanuphullos elaiēs); μέγα σῆμα τέτυκται (mega sēma tetuktai)
short: Odysseus built the bridal chamber around a growing olive tree and made its trunk the bed-post: 'a great token' known only to the couple.
body: Monro takes mega sēma tetuktai as 'there is in the making of the bedstead a secret that will serve for a token or pass-word'. He discusses akmēnos, 'in its prime', and notes Voss's preference for making the epithet tanuphullos ('long-leafed') agree with elaiē, the olive, as elsewhere (13.102). The olive is Athena's tree and recurs at key moments: Odysseus lands in Ithaca beside an olive at the harbour (13.102, 13.372), blinds the Cyclops with an olive stake (9.320), and the axe Calypso gives him has an olive handle (5.236). A bed rooted in the earth is an obvious image of an immovable marriage, built by the husband's own skill. Monro records an ancient variant reading, Hermes for herm(is) at 23.198, explained by a scholiast as a figure of Hermes, sender of dreams, carved on the bed-post.

title: The gods 'begrudged' their happiness
greek: θεοὶ δ' ὤπαζον ὀϊζύν, οἳ νῶϊν ἀγάσαντο (theoi d' ōpazon oizun, hoi nōin agasanto)
short: Penelope explains their sorrow as the gods' doing: the gods begrudged that they should enjoy their youth together and come to the threshold of old age.
body: Agamai means 'to wonder at, admire', and so 'to think something too much, to grudge'; Monro glosses agasanto as 'thought it too much', 'would not hear of it'. The idea that the gods resent excessive human good fortune, later called phthonos theōn, appears in Calypso's complaint that the gods are jealous of goddesses who love mortal men (5.118-20, where the same verb is used) and becomes a theme of Herodotus. Penelope's phrase 'the threshold of old age' (gēraos oudos) is formulaic (compare 15.246, 15.348). Her speech moves from blaming the gods to apology, and then to the comparison with Helen, which ancient critics found troubling.

title: Penelope's comparison with Helen (23.218-24)
greek: Ἀργείη Ἑλένη, Διὸς ἐκγεγαυῖα (Argeiē Helenē, Dios ekgegauia); ἄτη (atē)
short: Penelope says Helen would not have slept with a foreigner had she known the Achaeans would fetch her home; a god drove her to it. Aristarchus rejected these seven lines.
body: Monro sets out the debate. Aristarchus athetised 218-24, and most nineteenth-century critics agreed: Helen's case is not parallel to Penelope's, the excuse that a god compelled her is out of place, and the long parenthesis interrupts 'I was always afraid... but now' (23.215-25). A. Platt (Classical Review 13, 1899) defended the passage for its beauty and for the contrast, typical of the Odyssey, between Penelope and the unfaithful wife, as with Clytemnestra (11.405-56, 24.192-202), and for Penelope's generous excuse for Helen's atē, 'blind folly'. Monro finds the defence 'attractive, but somewhat fanciful', thinks the lines 'didactic rather than epic', and conjectures that they came from the Cypria, the cyclic epic of Helen's seduction. Many recent critics read the comparison as an apt self-justification: Penelope's caution is exactly what Helen lacked.

title: Actoris, keeper of the bridal chamber
greek: Ἀκτορίς (Aktoris)
short: The only person besides the couple to have seen the bed is a maid, 'the daughter of Actor', given to Penelope by her father when she married.
body: Aktoris is a patronymic form, 'daughter of Actor', and the maid is mentioned only here. Like the old servant Dolius, whom Icarius also gave Penelope when she came to Ithaca (4.735-7), she belongs to the dowry-servants who come with a bride. Monro glosses eiruto, 'guarded', 'was sentry at' the door. Her presence makes the secret of the bed a secret shared by three, which slightly complicates Penelope's 'signs which we two alone know' (23.110). It is also not clear how she relates to Eurynome, who leads the couple to the chamber at 23.289-93; readers have wondered whether the two are the same woman, but the text does not say so.

title: Reverse simile: Penelope as a shipwrecked swimmer
greek: ὡς δ' ὅτ' ἂν ἀσπάσιος γῆ νηχομένοισι φανήῃ (hōs d' hot' an aspasios gē nēchomenoisi phanēēi)
short: Her husband is as welcome to Penelope as land to shipwrecked men who swim ashore crusted with brine, a simile that gives the wife the experience of the husband.
body: The image fits Odysseus, not Penelope: Poseidon wrecked his raft and he swam to Scheria, his skin stripped by the rocks, crusted with salt (5.291-493). Applied to Penelope, it implies that her twenty years of waiting were a voyage and a shipwreck of their own. Helene Foley's influential study calls such comparisons 'reverse similes', in which a man is likened to a woman or a woman to a man, and argues that they express the reciprocity of Odysseus and Penelope; the pair at 19.108-14 (Penelope compared to a just king) is her other main case. The same Odysseus once wept 'like a woman' over her husband's body (8.523-31). The simile's final words, about the white arms she cannot let go, return the image to Penelope.

title: Athena holds back Dawn and her horses Lampus and Phaethon
greek: Λάμπον καὶ Φαέθοντα, οἵ τ' Ἠῶ πῶλοι ἄγουσι (Lampon kai Phaethonta, hoi t' Ēō pōloi agousi)
short: To give the couple time, Athena lengthens the night and keeps Dawn at the edge of Ocean, not letting her yoke her colts 'Bright' and 'Shining'.
body: Lampos and Phaethōn mean 'Shining' and 'Gleaming'; this is the only place in Homer where Dawn's horses are named. In the Iliad Hera does the opposite and sends the sun down early to end the fighting (Il. 18.239-42). Monro discusses the rare word peratē at 23.243, which Alexandrian scholars took to mean 'the far east'; he suggests instead a derivation from peraō, 'to pass', meaning the space the night crosses in its course. The divine intervention measures the occasion: after twenty years the night of reunion is granted extra hours, which the poem fills with love, stories and sleep.

title: Teiresias' prophecy: the oar mistaken for a winnowing fan
greek: ἀθηρηλοιγός (athērēloigos, 'chaff-destroyer'); ἐρετμόν (eretmon, oar)
short: Odysseus must journey inland carrying an oar until a stranger mistakes it for a winnowing fan, among people who know nothing of the sea and eat no salt.
body: The passage repeats Teiresias' instructions from 11.121-37 in indirect form. The athērēloigos, 'chaff-destroyer', is a winnowing shovel used to toss threshed grain so that the wind carries off the chaff; an oar and a winnowing fan look alike, and the point at which one is mistaken for the other marks the furthest limit of the sea's world. Monro notes that salt in Homeric times seems to have come only from the sea, and that 'know the sea' means 'know that there is such a thing'. He argues that the passage was designed to give 'a glimpse of the fortunes of Ulysses beyond' the poem, and that it sits uneasily with Book XXIV's ending. Sophocles' lost Odysseus Akanthoplēx, Monro observes, followed the prophecy closely.

title: A threefold sacrifice to Poseidon
greek: ἀρνειὸν ταῦρόν τε συῶν τ' ἐπιβήτορα κάπρον (arneion tauron te suōn t' epibētora kapron)
short: Where the oar is planted Odysseus must sacrifice a ram, a bull and a breeding boar to Poseidon, then go home and offer hecatombs to all the gods.
body: Monro compares the Roman suovetaurilia, the purificatory sacrifice of a pig (sus), a sheep (ovis) and a bull (taurus). Many scholars have read the whole prophecy as the means of reconciling Poseidon, who has persecuted Odysseus since the blinding of the Cyclops, by carrying his worship to a people who do not know the sea. Monro is sceptical: a seafaring man would naturally turn to Poseidon as his patron, and if the poet had meant a reconciliation, 'he would have told us that Poseidon was appeased by the sacrifice'. The later Telegony, as summarised by Proclus, says that after the suitors' burial Odysseus 'performs the sacrifices ordered by Teiresias', showing that the epic tradition took the instruction as part of Odysseus' future.

title: 'Death from the sea' or 'away from the sea'? (ex halos)
greek: θάνατος δέ μοι ἐξ ἁλὸς αὐτῷ ἀβληχρὸς μάλα τοῖος ἐλεύσεται (thanatos de moi ex halos autōi ablēchros mala toios eleusetai)
short: Murray translates 'far from the sea', but the Greek ex halos can also mean 'out of the sea', an ambiguity that later poets exploited.
body: Monro argues that ex halos with a verb of motion 'can only mean will come from the sea', the form of that death being left vague 'after the manner of prophecy'; elsewhere in Homer the phrase means 'out of the sea' (e.g. of Thetis rising from the sea, 24.47). He allows the possibility of a word exalos, 'away from the sea', which would make the point that the sailor dies on land. The Telegony told how Telegonus, Odysseus' son by Circe, landed on Ithaca from the sea and killed his father unknowingly, and later mythographers say the weapon was a spear tipped with a sting-ray's spine (Apollodorus, Epitome 7.36), a death literally 'from the sea'. The death is ablēchros, 'gentle' (Monro: by old age or Apollo's 'gentle arrows'), in 'sleek old age', with his people prosperous around him.

anchor: couch that was theirs of old
title: 'They came gladly to the rite of their old bed': the ancient 'end' of the Odyssey
greek: ἀσπάσιοι λέκτροιο παλαιοῦ θεσμὸν ἵκοντο (aspasioi lektroio palaiou thesmon hikonto)
short: According to the scholia, the Alexandrian scholars Aristophanes of Byzantium and Aristarchus called this line the 'end' of the Odyssey, a judgement still debated.
body: Thesmos occurs nowhere else in Homer; Monro takes it as 'place' or 'situation', though it can also mean 'rite, ordinance', and many readers hear in it the institution of marriage restored. A scholion reports that Aristophanes and Aristarchus regarded 23.296 as the peras or telos of the poem. Monro points out the puzzle that Aristarchus also athetised (marked as spurious) particular later passages (23.310-43, 24.1-204), and suggests he distinguished a later continuation from still later interpolations. He himself thinks the question must be decided by language and metre, and in his notes marks numerous late features in the continuation. Defenders reply that telos may mean 'goal' or 'climax' rather than 'last line', and that the poem needs Book XXIV to settle the blood-feud and reunite Odysseus with Laertes; Carroll Moulton surveys the arguments.

title: Odysseus' tale retold in brief (23.310-43)
greek: ἤρξατο δ' ὡς πρῶτον Κίκονας δάμασ' (ērxato d' hōs prōton Kikonas damas')
short: In bed Odysseus tells Penelope his whole story, from the Cicones to the Phaeacians, summarised in indirect speech: the 'tale to Alcinous' compressed into some thirty lines.
body: Aristotle cites the passage as a model of brevity: in the presence of Penelope the 'tale to Alcinous' (Books IX-XII) 'is reduced to sixty lines' (Rhetoric 3.16.7), apparently counting from memory, as Monro remarks, since the passage is about half that length. Aristarchus athetised it. Monro calls it 'strangely prosaic' and thinks it the work of a hand later even than the author of the continuation, pointing to non-Homeric forms such as ēēn (23.316) and the unusual use of hadinos of the Sirens (23.326). Others value it as the moment when Odysseus, the poem's great narrator, finally tells his true story to the one listener who matters, without lies or disguise; Penelope stays awake 'till he had told all the tale'.

title: Restocking by raiding
greek: πολλὰ μὲν αὐτὸς ἐγὼ ληΐσσομαι (polla men autos egō lēissomai)
short: Odysseus plans to replace the flocks the suitors devoured partly by raiding for booty himself and partly by gifts from the Achaeans.
body: Lēizomai means 'to carry off as booty' (lēis, plunder), and raiding other communities' herds was an accepted, even admired, way for a Homeric chieftain to build wealth. Odysseus' Cretan alter ego boasts of nine successful raids (14.229-34), and Nestor's youthful cattle raid on Elis is told with pride (Il. 11.670-84). Monro glosses epaulous as 'stalls' (Latin stabula). The remark shows that the restoration of the household is economic as well as moral, and it looks back to the young Odysseus' embassy to Messene to recover stolen sheep (21.16-21). Odysseus then orders Penelope to stay in her upper room and 'look on no man', in anticipation of the rumour that will spread at sunrise.

title: Athena hides them in darkness; a book-division mid-sentence
greek: τοὺς δ' ἄρ' Ἀθήνη νυκτὶ κατακρύψασα (tous d' ar' Athēnē nukti katakrupsasa)
short: Although it is already daylight, Athena covers Odysseus and his companions in darkness as they leave the city for Laertes' farm.
body: Divine concealment in mist or darkness is a frequent device in Homer (e.g. Athena around Odysseus entering the Phaeacian city, 7.14-17, 7.140). Monro notes that these two lines introduce the second Nekyia (24.1-204), and that the division between Books XXIII and XXIV falls in the middle of a sentence, as at some other book divisions (he compares 13.440 and 3.497). The book divisions of Homer are not the poet's own: they are usually attributed to Alexandrian scholars, who also named the books by the letters of the alphabet. The narrative of Odysseus' journey resumes at 24.205, after the scene in the underworld.
